svg.text: Stationary waves on strings, in air columns and with microwaves
Stationary waves on a stretched string (7.4, 7.5)

g.text: l = lambda1 / 2, lambda1 = 2l (7.2)
v = sqrt(F / m), m = mass per unit length (7.3)
n loops: n + 1 nodes, n antinodes; fn = n f1 (7.5)

svg.text: nodes lambda/2 apart; node to antinode lambda/4; energy stands between nodes
Stationary waves in air columns (7.6, Figs. 7.8, 7.9)

g.text: open end: antinode (air free to move); closed end: node
open: lambda1 = 2l (7.7), f1 = v/2l (7.8), fn = n f1, lambda_n = 2l/n (7.9)
closed: lambda1 = 4l (7.10), f1 = v/4l; lambda3 = 4l/3 (7.11), f3 = 3 f1;
lambda_n = 4l/n (7.12) with n odd: only odd harmonics
open pipe: all harmonics; closed pipe: only odd ones (open is richer)

svg.text: organ: an air jet from the flue-slit strikes the upper lip and drives the column

g.text: microwaves: electromagnetic, wavelength of mm to cm; the reflected waves superpose on
the incident waves to form a stationary pattern picked up by the probe; moving the probe
or plate finds nodes and antinodes; wavelength = 2 x (antinode-to-antinode distance)
microwave oven: a magnetron makes microwaves, a metal waveguide carries them, a rotating
stirrer spreads them; the metal box and the window's fine mesh keep them inside
harmonic series f1, 2 f1, 3 f1, ..., n f1: f1 is the fundamental
(first harmonic); only these are set up: quantization of frequency
tuning: change tension (pegs) or length (fingers on the neck)
Example 7.3: 1.2 m string, 4 loops at 120 Hz: lambda4 = 0.6 m,
Example 7.4: 0.5 m pipe, v = 350 m s^-1: open f1 = 350 Hz,
next 700 Hz; closed f1 = 175 Hz, next f3 = 525 Hz
Example 7.5: organ pipes open at one end, 30 mm to 4 m, v = 340:
f max = 2833 Hz, f min = 21.25 Hz
